summary: This informational memo defines extensions to the socket programming interface for the larger addresses and new features of IPv6. It was replaced by RFC 2553.

eli5.summary: A programmer's toolkit update so programs can use the new, longer Internet addresses.

subtitle: How programs ask the operating system to send and receive IPv6 messages.

tldr.problem: IPv6 addresses are 128 bits long, four times bigger than IPv4. Programs using the standard sockets API need changes to work with these larger addresses and IPv6's new features.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 2133 extends the sockets API with new address structures (sockaddr_in6), new library functions (getaddrinfo, getnameinfo), and socket options for multicast and hop limits.
tldr.outcome: Programs can use IPv6 networks with the same socket programming model they used for IPv4. This RFC was replaced by RFC 2553, which refined the API design.

today: RFC 2553 replaced this RFC in 1999, refining the socket API design based on implementation experience. RFC 2133 is marked Informational.

sections.title: The IPv6 Address Problem
sections.content:
The Internet had been using 32-bit addresses since the 1980s. When IPv6 added 128-bit addresses, every program that used the sockets API needed changes to handle these larger numbers. The sockets API is the standard way programs on Unix-like systems talk to the operating system to send and receive network data. RFC 2133 defines what those changes are.

The RFC had three design goals: keep existing IPv4 programs running unchanged, make the API changes as small as possible, and let new applications work with both IPv4 and IPv6 hosts without knowing which type they are talking to.
sections.eli5: IPv6 has much bigger address numbers than IPv4. The rules that let programs ask the operating system to send messages needed to be updated for these bigger numbers.

sections.title: IPv6 Address Structures
sections.content:
The core addition is a new data structure called sockaddr_in6. It holds six pieces of information: an address family identifier (set to AF_INET6), a 16-bit port number, a 32-bit flow label and priority field, and the 128-bit IPv6 address itself.

IPv6 also adds special addresses. The wildcard address (all zeros) works like the old INADDR_ANY constant in IPv4, letting the system choose a source address automatically. The loopback address (::1) lets programs on one computer talk to local services without sending anything over the network. These are provided both as variables and as initialization constants to match different coding styles.
sections.eli5: A new container holds the bigger address plus a port number and other information IPv6 needs. Special address numbers like 'any' and 'localhost' are provided so programs can use them like they did in IPv4.

sections.title: Creating and Using IPv6 Sockets
sections.content:
Programs create IPv6 sockets using the same socket() function they used for IPv4, but passing PF_INET6 instead of PF_INET to ask for IPv6. Once created, IPv6 sockets work with the same functions: bind() to assign a local address and port, connect() to open a connection, send() and receive() to exchange data.

The RFC defines socket options at the IPPROTO_IPV6 level to control behavior. The IPV6_UNICAST_HOPS option sets how many network hops a message can travel before being discarded (the hop limit). IPV6_MULTICAST_HOPS, IPV6_MULTICAST_IF, and IPV6_MULTICAST_LOOP control multicast packet sending. IPV6_ADD_MEMBERSHIP and IPV6_DROP_MEMBERSHIP let a program join and leave multicast groups. The IPV6_ADDRFORM option can convert a socket between IPv4 and IPv6 mode if needed.
sections.eli5: Programs use the same socket() function to create an IPv6 socket, just asking for IPv6 instead of IPv4. Socket options let programs control details like how far a message can travel or whether to join a group.

sections.title: Address Translation and Conversion
sections.content:
The RFC defines several library functions that programs use to work with IPv6 addresses. getaddrinfo() is the main one: given a hostname and service name, it returns a list of socket addresses to try. This is protocol-independent, so IPv6 applications can use the same code pattern as IPv4. The reverse function getnameinfo() converts a binary address and port back into a hostname and service name.

inet_pton() and inet_ntop() convert IPv6 addresses between binary form (as bytes, ready for the network) and text form (a string an engineer can read). inet_pton() takes a text string like "2001:db8::1" and turns it into 16 bytes. inet_ntop() does the reverse.

The RFC also defines address testing macros, such as IN6_IS_ADDR_MULTICAST(), to check if an address is loopback, multicast, link-local (meant only for the local network) or other special types. These let programs decide how to handle different categories of address without writing out byte-by-byte tests.
sections.eli5: The RFC adds functions to convert between human-friendly names like 'google.com' and the actual address bytes. It also provides shortcuts to check what type of address something is, like whether it is multicast or localhost.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and IPv4-Mapped Addresses
sections.content:
The RFC was designed to protect existing IPv4 programs. A system implementing RFC 2133 must still support PF_INET sockets and the old sockaddr_in structure. IPv4 applications should continue to work without any changes.

For cases where IPv6 programs need to talk to IPv4 hosts, the RFC introduces IPv4-mapped IPv6 addresses, a way to represent an IPv4 address as an IPv6 address. An IPv4 address like 192.0.2.1 becomes ::ffff:192.0.2.1 as an IPv6 address. An IPv6 application can pass this to connect() or sendto() to reach an IPv4 host, and the operating system handles the translation. The RFC provides a macro IN6_IS_ADDR_V4MAPPED() to test whether an address is one of these mapped addresses.
sections.eli5: Old IPv4 programs continue to work without changes. When an IPv6 program wants to talk to an old IPv4 computer, it can wrap the IPv4 address in a special IPv6 address format that the operating system understands.

sections.title: Interface and Multicast Functions
sections.content:
The RFC defines functions to work with network interfaces by index. if_nametoindex() converts an interface name like "eth0" to a small integer. if_indextoname() does the reverse. if_nameindex() returns all interfaces and their indexes. These are needed for multicast because multicast groups are tied to specific network interfaces.

For applications that need to know which local interface a datagram was received on (advanced use), or that need to send on a specific interface, this interface index mechanism provides a portable way to specify it.
sections.eli5: The RFC adds a way to identify which network cards are plugged into the computer by number. This is used when programs want to send multicast messages on a specific network card.
